school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Advanced Neurobiology II
description: In-depth coverage of neurobiology, ranging from molecular neurobiology to functional brain imaging. Discussion of systems and behavioral neurobiology.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N115A
restriction: Neurobiology majors only

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Introduction to Neuroscience Clinical Trials
description: Provides an overview of the science of clinical development of treatments for neurological disease and injury.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 99

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Clinical Psychophysiology
description: Psychophysiology investigates the relationships between physiological processes and psychological phenomena. Technologies examined include reaction times, heart rate variability, EEGs, ERPs, magnetoencephalography, and eye tracking. Applications include diagnosis, the longitudinal assessment, and the identification of individuals at risk of disease onset.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A or PSYCH 9A or PSCI 11A

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: History of Neuroscience
description: An overview of the conceptual and technical foundations of contemporary neuroscience from ancient times to the present. The subjects include synapses, neurons, brain organization, sensory, motor and regulatory systems, learning and memory, human brain function and dysfunction.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 35 or BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A or PSY BEH 115D or (PSYCH 9A and PSYCH 9B and PSYCH 9C)

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Human Biology
description: Human Biology provides an in-depth look at cutting edge topics in physiology and epidemiology as they relate to global issues of ethics, anthropology, and socioeconomics, providing the student an understanding of human health beyond basic biological function.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 99.
restriction: Human Biology majors only.

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Human Biology I
description: Provides an in-depth look at cutting-edge topics in physiology and epidemiology as they relate to global issues of ethics, anthropology, and socioeconomics, providing the student with an understanding of human health beyond basic biological function.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 99
restriction: Human Biology majors only

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Human Biology II
description: Provides an in-depth look at cutting-edge topics in physiology and epidemiology as they relate to global issues of ethics, anthropology, and socioeconomics, providing the student with an understanding of human health beyond basic biological function.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N120A
restriction: Human Biology majors only

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Human Biology III
description: Provides an in-depth look at cutting-edge topics in physiology and epidemiology as they relate to global issues of ethics, anthropology, and socioeconomics, providing the student with an understanding of human health beyond basic biological function.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N120B
restriction: Human Biology majors only

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Drug Addiction
description: Provides a comprehensive overview of topics in the addiction field, including drug pharmacology, models/approaches to investigate addiction, brain circuits, genetics, epigenetics, and the cellular and molecular biology of drug addiction.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 99

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Scientific Argumentation and Critical Thinking
description: Explicitly teaches argument structure, deductive logic, inductive logic, and common fallacies in the biology context. Students identify assumptions and fallacies in faulty arguments and data figures and learn to compose sound arguments.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 93. Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Human Neuroimaging Lab
description: Hands-on laboratory course in human neuroimaging, with particular emphasis on using MRI to understand brain function and how it changes over the course of the lifespan and with disease.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 93 and (BIO SCI 100 or BIO SCI 108). Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement
restriction: Seniors have the first consideration for enrollment. Students who require this lab for completion of their degree have first consideration for enrollment

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Model Systems in Biology
description: On the use of animal and in vitro models in biomedical research, focusing on assumptions, promises, limitations, and compromises.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 93

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Foundations in Neuroimmunology
description: The immune system supports normal brain development as well as controls central nervous system (CNS) infections and augments neurodegenerative and neurological diseases. Assesses how the immune system contributes to both host defense and disease.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI M121

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Into the Human Brain
description: Explores different methods for studying the human brain in vivo (EEG, MRI, TMS, and others). Discusses ways to measure and manipulate brain activity directly and indirectly and how these different approaches complement each other.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 99

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: The Transparent Brain
description: Teaches students how to perform new 3-D histology techniques that reveal the complex circuitry of the brain in unprecedented detail. Students work with real brain samples as part of ongoing neuroscience research projects. Materials fee.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 93 or BIO SCI H93
restriction: Students who require this course for completion of their degree have first consideration for enrollment.

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Human Neurodegenerative Diseases
description: Clinical and epidemiological aspects of neurodegenerative diseases causing dementia are reviewed, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, Huntington’s disease, and Frontotemporal Dementia. Seminar format includes student presentation and group discussion.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 99

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Cognitive Neuroepigenetics
description: Current topics in the emerging field of cognitive neuroepigenetics focusing on understanding the underlying epigenetic mechanisms of memory formation and persistence. Primary literature is used to explore these processes.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Sex Differences in the Brain
description: Explores the neural bases of sex influences on brain function.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 99

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Hearing and the Brain
description: An overview of brain mechanisms of hearing, including perception of simple sounds, speech, and music. Begins with sound itself, and looks at processing by the ear, auditory pathways, auditory cortex, and beyond. Also auditory development, learning, and clinical issues.

instructors.name: Raju Metherate
instructors.title: Professor and Associate Dean of Undergraduate Education

prerequisiteText: COGS 160A or BIO SCI 93 or BIO SCI H93
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors, Psychology majors, and School of Biological Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Brain Dysfunction and Repair
description: Introduction to the disruptions in brain function that underlie disorders such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinsonism, schizophrenia, and depression, and the basis for drug therapies. The brain's ability to repair itself after damage and the pros and cons of that repair.

instructors.name: Frank M Laferla
instructors.title: Dr. Lionel and Fay Ng Dean
instructors.department: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences

prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A
restriction: Neurobiology Majors only.

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Neurobiology of Aging
description: Multidisciplinary overview of the functional capacity of the aging brain, its structural changes and the mechanisms underlying function and structure. Emphasis is on successful brain aging and those mechanisms which lead to the development of Alzheimer's disease.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Developmental Neurobiology
description: The development of the nervous system is discussed with emphasis on the processes that underlie the appearance of complex and highly ordered neural circuits. Topics include neural induction, specification, migration and death; axon growth, and neural circuit formation.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 93 or BIO SCI H93

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Neuropharmacology
description: Survey of neurotransmitter systems, focusing on how transmitters are made, how they interact with their receptors, and how drugs can influence these processes to alter neural function and behavior.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Molecular Neurobiology
description: Provides a fundamental understanding of how the brain works at the molecular level. Topics include nature and actions of molecules that regulate the functioning of the brain and cellular mechanisms underlying learning and memory.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 99

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Wiring the Developing Brain
description: The development of the nervous system is discussed with particular emphasis on the processes that underlie the appearance of complex and highly ordered neural circuits. Basic neurodevelopmental processes are discussed and correlated with normal brain function/dysfunction.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A or BIO SCI N152

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Molecular Mechanisms of Memory
description: Current topics focused on understanding the molecular mechanisms that contribute to synaptic plasticity, learning, and memory. Primary literature is used to explore the variety of molecular mechanisms underlying these processes.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 99

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Neurobiology of Learning and Memory
description: How the brain and behavior change as a result of experience, with an emphasis on identifying the neurochemical processes through which memory is stored and the parts of the brain that are involved.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 35 or BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Animal Behavior
description: Explores why animals behave the way they do from evolutionary/mechanistic perspectives. Considers selective pressures and evolutionary constraints that shape animal behavior and the underlying neural and hormonal mechanisms by using examples such as why dogs bark, why some birds migrate.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Language and the Brain
description: Research analysis on biological bases of human linguistic capacity. Development, focusing on hemispheric specialization, plasticity; localization of specific linguistic functions in adults, with emphasis on study of aphasias; relation of linguistic capacity to general cognitive capacity, considering research on retardation.

instructors.name: Gregory Hickok
instructors.title: Distinguished Professor & Department Chair of Language Science

prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or (COGS 9A or PSCI 11A) and (COGS 9B or PSCI 11B) or BIO SCI 35 or BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors, Biological Sciences majors, Psychology majors, and Language Science majors have the first consideration for enrollment

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Functional Neuroanatomy
description: How neuroscience uses tools of many disciplines, from imaging to behavior, to develop and test hypotheses about functions of specific parts of the brain. Basic organization of nerve cells/vertebrate nervous system; methods of visualizing nerve cells; neural connections/activity patterns.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI 99

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Brain Disorders and Behavior
description: Examines the localization of human brain functions and the effects of neurological disorders on psychological functions such as perception, motor control, language, memory, and decision-making.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or (COGS 9A or PSCI 11A) and (COGS 9B or PSCI 11B) or BIO SCI 35 or BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A
restriction: Biological Sciences majors, Cognitive Sciences majors, and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Introduction to Cognitive Neuroscience
description: Introduction to the neural basis of human perceptual, motor, and cognitive abilities. Topics include sensory perception, motor control, memory, language, attention, emotion, frontal lobe function, functional brain imaging, and neuropsychological disorders.
prerequisiteText: PSYCH 7A or (PSYCH 9A and PSYCH 9B) or PSY BEH 9 or (PSY BEH 11A and PSY BEH 11B) or BIO SCI 35 or BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Clinical Neuroscience
description: An introduction to the neuroclinical bases of human behavior, including neuropsychological approaches to mental disorders. Also includes case formulations, research articles, therapeutic approaches, and other discussions related to select psychopathology and other neurobehavioral topics.
prerequisiteText: Recommended: PSCI 9 or PSYCH 7A or PSCI 11A or PSYCH 9A or BIO SCI 99
restriction: Psychological Science majors, Psychology and Social Behavior majors, Social Ecology majors, and School of Biological Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Regenerative Neurobiology
description: Explores the field of regenerative neurobiology. Both basic stem cell discoveries and their potential clinical application to brain disorders examined. Opportunities, challenges, and implications of this research also discussed.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Human Neuropsychology
description: A survey of human brain disorders using a clinical case study approach to illustrate fundamental issues in studying brain and behavior. Topics include sensory deficits, attentional neglect, amnesia, cortical organization, clinical psychopathology, and more.

instructors.name: Michael A Yassa
instructors.title: Professor & Associate Dean of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion

prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A or COGS 9A or PSCI 11A
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors, Psychological Science majors, Psychology majors, and School of Biological Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Principles of Neural Computation
description: Introduction to the theoretical principles and biological mechanisms underlying how brains acquire, assimilate, store, and retrieve information, and how they compute adaptive responses to external inputs.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Cerebral Cortex: Structure, Function, and Plasticity
description: The cerebral cortex is highly developed in mammals and is responsible for higher perceptual and cognitive functions. Explores some amazing aspects of cortical structure, function, and plasticity emphasizing primary literature.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Vision
description: Visual perception and the anatomy and physiology of the visual system. Topics include the retina and the visual pathway; visual sensitivity; color vision; spatial vision; motion perception; and the development of the visual system.
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors, Psychology majors, and School of Biological Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment

school: Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences
title: Topics in Neurobiology and Behavior
description: Studies in selected areas of neurobiology and behavior.

Principles of problem solving, design, engineering inventiveness, entrepreneurship, information access, communication, ethics, teamwork, and social responsibility are emphasized.

description: Introduction to statics and dynamics. Topics include rigid bodies, analysis of structures, forces in beams, moments of inertia, friction, kinetics, work, and energy.

description: Introduction to biomechanics from subcellular to tissue levels. Introduction to stress, strain, and constitutive laws of cells and tissues. Emphasis is placed on biosolids. Introduction to elastic and viscoelastic behaviors with emphasis on the standard linear model of viscoelasticity.

restriction: Biomedical Engineering majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Design of Biomaterials
description: Natural and synthetic polymeric materials. Metal and ceramics implant materials. Mechanical properties, degradation, surface characterization, and design of materials. Wound repair, blood clotting, foreign body response, biocompatibility of material. Artificial organs and medical devices. Government regulations.
prerequisiteText: (BME 50B or BIO SCI 99) and CHEM 1C
restriction: Biomedical Engineering majors, Biomedical Engineering: Premedical majors, and Materials Science and Engineering majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Finite Element Modeling for Bioengineers
description: Introduction to finite-element simulation; fundamentals of Multiphysics simulation; essential skills in performing simulations with COMSOL®.
prerequisiteText: BME 60B and BME 60C and BME 110A
restriction: Biomedical Engineering majors and Biomedical Engineering: Premedical majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Genetic Engineering and Synthetic Biology
description: Exploring how biological function can be engineered and "synthesized" from the DNA level up.
prerequisiteText: (CHEM 1C or CHEM H2C) and MATH 3D and BME 50A and BME 50B
restriction: Biomedical Engineering majors have the first consideration for enrollment

description: A quantitative and systems approach to understanding physiological systems. Systems covered include the nervous and musculoskeletal systems.

description: Analysis of analog and digital biomedical signals; Fourier Series expansions; difference and differential equations; convolutions. System models: discrete-time and continuous-time linear time-invariant systems; Laplace and Fourier transforms. Analysis of signals and systems using computer programs.
prerequisiteText: BME 60B and (MATH 3A or I&C SCI 6N) and MATH 3D. Recommended: STATS 8
restriction: Biomedical Engineering majors and Biomedical Engineering: Premedical majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Introduction to Computational Biology
description: The use of theories and methods based on computer science, mathematics, and physics in molecular biology and biochemistry. Basics in biomolecular modeling. Analysis of sequence and structural data of biomolecules. Analysis of biomolecular functions.
prerequisiteText: MATH 2D or MATH 3A or STATS 7 or STATS 8

title: Photomedicine
description: Studies the use of optical and engineering-based systems (laser-based) for diagnosis, treating diseases, manipulation of cells and cell function. Physical, optical, and electro-optical principles are explored regarding molecular, cellular, organ, and organism applications.

description: Principles of optics and photonics, integration of optical components into systems and devices, and analysis of physiological signals obtained from Biophotonics measurements.
prerequisiteText: PHYSICS 7E or PHYSICS 3C
restriction: Biomedical Engineering majors and Biomedical Engineering: Premedical majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Introduction to Biomedical Imaging
description: Introduction to imaging modalities widely used in medicine and biology, including X-ray, computed tomography (CT), nuclear medicine (PET and SPET), ultrasonic imaging, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), optical tomography, imaging contrast, imaging processing, and complementary nature of the imaging modalities.
prerequisiteText: BME 130 or EECS 50 or EECS 150
restriction: Biomedical Engineering majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Spectroscopy and Imaging of Biological Systems
description: Principles of spectroscopy; absorption; molecular orbitals; multiphoton transitions; Jablonski diagram; fluorescence anisotropy; fluorescence decay; quenching; FRET; excited state reactions; solvent relaxations; instruments; microscopy: wide field, LSM, TPE; fluorescent probes, fluctuations spectroscopy; optical resolution and super-resolution; CARS and SHG microscopy.
prerequisiteText: (MATH 3A or I&C SCI 6N) and MATH 3D. Recommended: STATS 8
restriction: Biomedical Engineering majors and Biomedical Engineering: Premedical majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Design of Biomedical Electronics
description: Analog and digital circuits in bioinstrumentation. AC and DC circuit analysis, design and construction of filter and amplifiers using operational amplifier, digitization of signals and data acquisition, bioelectrical signals, design and construction of ECG instrument, bioelectrical signal measurement and analysis. Materials Fee
prerequisiteText: BME 60A and BME 130
restriction: Biomedical Engineering majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Microfabrication
description: Essentials of photolithography, soft-lithography, microfabrication, Microelectromechanical Systems (MEMS), BioMEMS; applications in biomedical engineering.
restriction: Biomedical Engineering majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Microfluidics and Lab-on-a-Chip
description: Introduction to principles of microfluidics and state-of-the-art micro Total Analysis Systems (uTAS). Lab-on-a-Chip for bimolecular assays with device design principles for microscale sample preparation, flow transport, bimolecular manipulation, separation and detection, and the technologies for integrating these devices into microsystems.
prerequisiteText: BME 110C
restriction: Biomedical Engineering majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Microimplants
description: Essential concepts of biomedical implants at the micro scale. Design, fabrication, and applications of several microimplantable devices including cochlear, retinal, neural, and muscular implants.
prerequisiteText: BME 111
restriction: Biomedical Engineering majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Biomedical Microdevices
description: In-depth review of microfabricated devices designed for biological and medical applications. Studies of the design, implementation, manufacturing, and marketing of commercial and research bio-medical devices.

title: Biotransport Phenomena
description: Fundamentals of heat and mass transfer, similarities in the respective rate equations. Emphasis on practical application of fundamental principles.

description: Quantitative analysis of cell and tissue functions. Emerging developments in stem cell technology, biodegradable scaffolds, growth factors, and others important in developing clinical products. Applications of bioengineering.

description: A broad picture of diverse modern bioengineering tools, including genetic engineering and its risks to society, how to sequence DNA/RNA molecules with single base resolution, how to manipulate small biomolecules one at a time.

prerequisiteText: BME 220 with a minimum grade of B- and BME 221 with a minimum grade of B-

restriction: Graduate student only.

title: Directed Evolution
description: Directed evolution harnesses the processes of Darwinian evolution for biomolecular engineering goals. This class will begin with fundamental principles in evolutionary biology and move on to the experimental evolution techniques and their applications.
restriction: Graduate students only.

title: Organ Transport Systems

restriction: Master of Engineering only

title: Biofluid Mechanics

title: Molecular and Cellular Biophotonics

Sample technologies Optical Tweezers, Linear and Nonlinear Optical Microscopy and Fluorescence Lifetime and Correlation Methods, and their use to investigate emergent problems in Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology.
restriction: Graduate students only.

title: Tissue and Organ Biophotonics
description: Principles underlying the application of photonic technologies to tissues, organs, organisms. Sample technologies include Optical Coherence Tomography, Optical Speckle Imaging, Optoacoustic Imaging, Wide-Field Spectroscopic Imaging, Diffuse Optical Spectroscopy. Addressing the use of these technologies to detect/monitor disease and physiological processes.

title: Applied Engineering Mathematics I

Analytical and computational tools are used to model and analyze dynamic systems such as population, neuronal and heart dynamics, biochemical and physiological systems, oxygen diffusion and similar.

description: Fundamentals of optical system design, integration, and analysis used in biomedical optics. restriction: Graduate students only.

description: Introduction to Cuban history, culture, and society using social science texts, visual and musical materials. Examines major historical moments including the historical relationship between the United States and explores evolution of Cuban music from the earliest times to present.

title: Histories of Chicana/o/x and Latina/o/x Struggles for Civil Rights, 1960-1980
description: Provides students with an opportunity to learn more about the historical, political, and social underpinnings that oriented the civil rights struggles of mid-to-late 20th-century Chicana/o/x and Latina/o/x activists.

title: Black Latinidades
description: Questions the parameters of Latinidad by centering the origins and development of African descent communities in the Americas through a multidisciplinary, transnational, and diasporic approach to the study of Afro-Latinidad.

title: Chicana/Chicano History: Pre-Colonial to 1900
description: Examines social history of the southwest region from antiquity to 1900. Discusses major questions, theory and research methods pertinent to Chicanas/Chicanos. Themes include: indigenous empires, conquest, colonialism, social stratification, ideology, marriage, sexuality, industrial capitalism, accommodation and resistance.

title: Chicana/Chicano History: Twentieth Century
description: Examines social history of the Southwest with emphasis on Mexican-origin people. Discusses major questions, theory and research methods pertinent to Chicana/Chicano history. Themes explored include: immigration, xenophobia, class struggle, leadership, generational cohorts, unionization, education, barrioization, ethnicity, patriarchy, sexuality.

title: Interdisciplinary Legacies
description: Students learn from the institutional histories and scholarship of the Chicano/Latino Studies faculty emeriti who founded the Department and contributed to its scholarly presence and impact.

title: Twentieth-Century Mexico
description: Examines the history of contemporary Mexico beginning with the Mexican Revolution and concluding with the present administration. Social, economic, and political effects of the Revolution; formation of a "one-party democracy"; economic transformation of the nation; the present crisis.

title: U.S. Latino Literature and Cultures
description: Focuses on aspects of literature, art, cultural production, and history of the multifaceted Latino cultures that have developed within the United States. Focuses on one group, such as Caribbean Americans, Chicanos, Central Americans, or a comparative perspective of several groups.

title: Latinas in the Twentieth Century U.S.
description: Latinas in the U.S. from 1900 to present, offering a diversity of their cultures, regional histories, sexualities, generations, and classes.

title: Comparative Latino Populations
description: Provides foundation for understanding of Chicano/Latino Studies as an interdisciplinary field of inquiry. Focus on the history, arts, cultures of distinct (Mexican, Cuban, Puerto Rican, Central American) Latino communities. Topics include: precolonial history and culture, conquest, mestizaje, colonialism/neocolonialism, resistance.

title: Chicano/Chicana Labor History
description: Examines origins of Latino/ Latina labor from colonial period to present. Emphasis on the issues of race, culture, class, and gender. Focus on processes and institutions including: encomienda, migration, unions, informal economies, Bracero program, domestic work.

description: Examines a range of theoretical, empirical, and policy approaches to legal issues affecting the Latino population, with emphasis on California. Discusses topics concerning the purpose of law, the creation of law, and the enforcement of law.

title: Latinx Racial Formations
description: Students explore the meanings attributed to Latina/o/x racial identities over time; the political, economic, and social structures that have shaped those identities; and their impact on Latinx self-concepts, interpersonal/intra-community relations, and life chances.

title: Comparative Minority Politics
description: Examines the political experiences of Blacks, Latinos, and Asian Americans in the United States from roughly 1950 to the present. Focuses on how each group has pursued political empowerment via both conventional political channels and social movements.

description: Explores political, economic, social, and cultural ties that bind Latin America to the United States. Focuses on U.S. intervention and Latin American response from early nineteenth century to present day. Case studies include Mexico, Guatemala, Cuba, Chile, and Central America.

title: Sex and Conquest in Latin America
description: Competing ideas of masculinity and femininity, sexual violence, sexual identities, and gendered hierarchies informed how the Spanish engaged in military and religious domination of Mexican and Andean communities, as well as the forms of native resistance throughout colonial Latin America.

title: Latinos in U.S. Politics
description: Comparing the political issues facing Latino groups by examining their migration histories, voting behavior, nonelectoral participation, and policy issues. Latino issues are examined on the national, state, and local levels, including formal representation, immigration, affirmative action, and language policy.

description: Introduces the main concepts and theoretical approaches underlying the study of Latin American politics, examines recent political dynamics, and explores the challenges the region faces in the twenty-first century and how countries will attempt to address them.

title: Revolution in Latin America
description: Presents a comparative analysis of the causes, development, and consequences of selected revolutionary movements, focusing on outbreaks in Mexico, Bolivia, Cuba, Chile, Nicaragua, and Grenada. Explores topics of state formation, economic nationalism, social justice, ethnicity, and role of international affairs.

title: Race, Ethnicity, and Social Control
description: Provides a historical and sociological survey of racial and ethnic group relations in contexts of crime control, emphasizing the roles of racial ideology, structural racism, and social movements in shaping these dynamic relations, and their significance to American liberal democracy.
restriction: Chicano/Latino Studies majors, Criminology, Law and Society majors, and Social Ecology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Community, Social Justice, and Health Equity Research for Action

restriction: Criminology, Law and Society Majors have first consideration for enrollment. SocEcol-Urban & Regional Plan Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Chicano/Latino Studies Majors have first consideration for enrollment.

description: Explores the processes of Latino urbanization in the United States and the spatialization of Latino identities, particularly in the context of Southern California with selected comparisons drawing from other cities.

description: Explores theories that explain the occupational pathways and workplace experiences of Latinos in various work sectors. Investigates jobs such as migrant labor, child street vendors, Latina/Latino professionals, and Latinos migrating to the U.S. South that work in poultry processing plants.

description: Origins and organization of racialized social control, with emphasis on criminal justice. title: Conduct of Research
description: Introduces new graduate students to ethical conduct of scientific research, mentoring, and current research in the Department of Chemistry.
repeatability: May be taken for credit 2 times

title: Organic Reaction Mechanisms I
description: Advanced treatment of basic mechanistic principles of modern organic chemistry. Topics include molecular orbital theory, orbital symmetry control of organic reactions, aromaticity, carbonium ion chemistry, free radical chemistry, the chemistry of carbenes and carbanions, photochemistry, electrophilic substitutions, aromatic chemistry.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 132A and CHEM 132B and CHEM 132C

title: Organic Reaction Mechanisms II
description: Topics include more in-depth treatment of mechanistic concepts, kinetics, conformational analysis, computational methods, stereoelectronics, and both solution and enzymatic catalysis.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 201 with a minimum grade of B-

title: Organic Spectroscopy
description: Modern methods used in structure determination of organic molecules. Topics include mass spectrometry; ultraviolet, chiroptical, infrared, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy.
prerequisiteText: (CHEM 51A and CHEM 51B and CHEM 51C) or (CHEM H52A and CHEM H52B and CHEM H52C)

title: Organic Synthesis I
description: Fundamentals of modern synthetic organic chemistry is developed. Major emphasis is on carbon-carbon bond forming methodology. Topics include carbonyl annelations, cycloadditions, sigmatropic rearrangements, and organometallic methods.

title: Organic Synthesis II
description: Fundamentals of modern synthetic organic chemistry will be developed. Major emphasis this quarter is on natural product total synthesis and retrosynthetic (antithetic) analysis.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 204 with a minimum grade of B-

title: Advanced Data Acquisition and Analysis
description: Introduces students to a variety of practical laboratory techniques, including lock-in, boxcar, coincidence counting, noise filtering, PID control, properties of common transducers, computer interfacing to instruments, vacuum technology, laboratory safety, basic mechanical design, and shop skills. Materials Fee

title: Applied Physical Chemistry
description: Introduction to fundamental concepts in molecular structure and reactivity: theory of bonding, valence and molecular orbitals; structure and reactivity in inorganic chemistry; elements in molecular group theory; nomenclature in organic chemistry; and survey of macromolecules.

title: Math Methods
description: Applications of mathematics to physical and chemical problems. Calculus of special functions, complex variables and vectors; linear vector spaces and eigenvalue problems. Differential equations.

title: Physics for Chemists
description: An introduction to concepts of electrodynamics with special emphasis on applications to chemistry: vector analysis, electrostatics, magnetostatics, electrodynamics, electromagnetic waves, classical radiation theory, special relativity.

title: Chemical Kinetics
description: Surveys gas phase and organic reaction mechanisms and their relationship to kinetic rate laws; treats the basic theory of elementary reaction rates. A brief presentation of modern cross-sectional kinetics is included.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 132A and CHEM 132B and CHEM 132C

title: Inorganic Chemistry I
description: Principles of modern inorganic chemistry with applications to chemical systems of current interest. Inorganic phenomena are organized into general patterns which rationalize observed structures, stabilities, and physical properties.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 107 and CHEM 132A and CHEM 132B and CHEM 132C

title: Organometallic Chemistry
description: Synthesis and reactivity of organometallic complexes with an emphasis on mechanisms. Topics include bonding and fluxional properties; metal-carbon single and multiple bonds; metal š-complexes. Applications to homogenous catalysis and organic synthesis are incorporated throughout the course.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 107 or CHEM 215 with a minimum grade of B-

title: Physical Inorganic Chemistry
description: General principles of the spectroscopy and magnetism of inorganic compounds. Characterization of inorganic complexes by infrared, near-infrared, visible, ultraviolet, NMR, EPR, EXAFS, and Mossbauer spectroscopies. Some necessary group theory developed.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 215 with a minimum grade of B-

title: Metallobiochemistry
description: A review of the biochemistry of metallic elements emphasizing: methods for studying metals in biological systems; the chemical basis for nature's exploitation of specific elements; structures of active sites; mechanisms; solid-state structures and devices; metals in medicine.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 131C (may be taken concurrently) or CHEM 132C (may be taken concurrently)

title: Chemical and Structural Biology
description: A survey of the organic chemistry underlying biological function. Introduction to chemical genetics, receptor-ligand interactions, small molecule agonists and antagonists, combinatorial synthesis, high throughput assays, molecular evolution, protein and small molecule design.

title: Advanced Chemical Biology
description: Modern topics in chemical biology, with an emphasis on application of principles from organic chemistry to biological research and biotechnology. Topics include methods to generate, identify, and manipulate major classes of biomolecules including nucleic acids, carbohydrates, lipids, and secondary metabolites.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 219 with a minimum grade of B-

title: Fundamentals of Molecular Biophysics
description: An overview of the principles and concepts in molecular biophysics. Topics covered include energy and entropy in biology, non-equilibrium reaction kinetics, random walks and molecular diffusion, molecular forces in biology.
prerequisiteText: Undergraduate courses in physical chemistry and biochemistry
repeatability: May be taken for credit 3 times

title: Biological Macromolecules
description: Introduction to nucleic acid and protein structure, dynamics, and function. Topics include analytical methods, molecular evolution, folding, and catalysis.

title: Molecular and Cellular Biophotonics
description: Principles underlying the application of photonic technologies to biomolecular and cellular systems. Sample technologies Optical Tweezers, Linear and Nonlinear Optical Microscopy and Fluorescence Lifetime and Correlation Methods, and their use to investigate emergent problems in Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology.
restriction: Graduate students only.

title: Polymer Chemistry: Synthesis and Characterization of Polymers
description: Structure of synthetic and natural polymers. Survey of modern polymer synthetic methods. Molecular weight and molecular weight distribution. Chain conformation and stereochemistry. Introduction to polymer characterization, chain models, and solution behavior.
prerequisiteText: Undergraduate courses in organic and physical chemistry

title: Electromagnetism
description: Maxwell’s equations, electrodynamics, electromagnetic waves and radiation, wave propagation in media, interference and quantum optics, coherent and incoherent radiation, with practical applications in interferometry, lasers, waveguides, and optical instrumentation.

title: Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences
description: Mathematical and numerical analysis using Mathematica and C programming, as applied to problems in physical science.

title: Computational Methods
description: Mathematical and numerical analysis using Mathematica and C programming, as applied to problems in physical science.

title: Classical Mechanics and Electromagnetic Theory
description: Fundamentals of classical mechanics and electromagnetic theory are developed with specific application to molecular systems. Newtonian, Lagrangian, and Hamiltonian mechanics are developed. Boundary value problems in electrostatics are investigated. Multipole expansion and macroscopic media are discussed from a molecular viewpoint.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 132A and CHEM 132B and CHEM 132C

title: Fundamentals of Quantum Mechanics
description: The postulates of quantum mechanics are discussed and applied to a variety of model problems.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 131A and CHEM 131B and CHEM 131C

title: Applications of Quantum Mechanics
description: Approximate methods for solving atomic and molecular structure problems are developed, and the application of quantum mechanics to spectroscopy is introduced.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 231A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Molecular Spectroscopy
description: Theory and techniques of spectroscopy as used for the study of molecular and condensed phase properties. Coherent time domain spectroscopies are covered.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 231B with a minimum grade of B-

title: Thermodynamics and Introduction to Statistical Mechanics
description: A detailed discussion from an advanced point of view of the principles of classical thermodynamics. The fundamentals of statistical mechanics. Topics include an introduction to ensemble theory, Boltzmann statistics, classical statistical mechanics, and the statistical mechanics of ideal gas systems.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 131A and CHEM 131B and CHEM 131C

prerequisites.title: Molecular Structure and Elementary Statistical Mechanics

title: Advanced Topics in Statistical Mechanics
description: Continued discussion of the principles of statistical mechanics. Applications to topics of chemical interest including imperfect gases, liquids, solutions, and crystals. Modern techniques such as the use of autocorrelation function methods.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 232A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Non-Equilibrium Statistical Mechanics
description: Phenomenology of material processes, including: kinetic theories of transport and continuum, linear response theory, critical phenomena of phase transition, self-assembly, and nucleation.

title: Nuclear and Radiochemistry
description: Advanced treatment of nuclear structure, nuclear reactions, and radioactive-decay processes. Introduction to nuclear activation analysis, isotope effects, radiation chemistry, hot-atom chemistry, nuclear age-dating methods, nuclear reactors, and nuclear power.

title: Advanced Chemical Kinetics
description: Topics and format vary.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 213.
repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

title: Molecular Quantum Mechanics
description: Application of quantum mechanics to calculation of molecular properties. Electronic structure of molecules.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 231A

title: Forces Between Molecules
description: The nature and effects of non-covalent interactions between molecular systems. The focus is on properties of these interactions in condensed phases: macromolecular systems; particle-surface interactions.

title: Mathematical Methods in Chemistry
description: Survey of essential math methods in chemistry. Topics may include series and limits, complex analysis, Fourier and Laplace transforms, linear algebra and operators (theory and algorithms), differential equations, and probability concepts for stochastic processes.

title: Special Topics in Density Functional Theory
description: Advanced topics in density functional theory.
prerequisiteText: One year of graduate quantum mechanics, or the equivalent
repeatability: May be taken unlimited times as topics vary

title: Machine Learning in Chemistry
description: Introductory course in machine learning, accessible to any graduate student in chemistry. Covers the basics of theory and practice of machine learning in modern chemistry. No coding or previous experience required.
prerequisiteText: Must be familiar with standard computer operation

title: Current Issues Related to Air Quality, Climate, and Energy
description: Current issues related to the atmosphere, climate, and air quality in the context of energy conversion and sustainability. Topics include transportation systems; building design; impacts on humans and ecosystems; modeling and meteorology; economics; and application to public policies.

title: Physical and Geometrical Optics
description: Focuses on the practical aspects of optics and optical engineering, starting at the fundamentals. Topics include geometrical optics, ray tracing, polarization optics, interferometers, and diffractive optics.
restriction: Graduate students only.

title: Applied Optics
description: Focuses on the treatment of a wide variety of tools and techniques used in optics, particularly in research. Subjects include an introduction to lasers, optical detection, coherent optics, spectroscopic techniques, and selected topics corresponding to the interest of the students.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 242A

title: Advanced Instrumental Analysis
description: Theory and applications of modern advanced instrumental methods of analysis. Includes data acquisition, storage, retrieval, and analysis; Fourier transform methods; vacuum technologies; magnetic sector; quadrupole and ion trap mass spectrometry; surface science spectroscopic methods; lasers and optics.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 152 with a minimum grade of B and CHEM 132C with a minimum grade of B

title: Detection and Measurement of Radiation
description: Basic principles of detection and measurement of ionizing radiation; both theory and practical aspects of measurement techniques for alpha, beta, gamma, and neutron radiation, properties of different detector materials, electronics and data treatments, and analysis.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 233 with a minimum grade of B- or CBE 276 with a minimum grade of B-

title: Atmospheric Chemistry of the Natural and Polluted Troposphere
description: Kinetics, mechanisms and photochemistry of tropospheric reactions in the gas, liquid, and solid phases, and methods of analysis. Chemistry of photochemical oxidant formation and acid deposition, and applications to control strategies. Chemistry of toxic chemicals and indoor air pollution.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 131A and CHEM 131B and CHEM 131C.

title: Gas-Phase Atmospheric Chemistry
description: Sources, chemistry, sinks, and measurements of key atmospheric gaseous species. Chemistry of photochemical oxidant formation, transformation of key inorganic and organic trace gases, and stratospheric ozone cycling. Applications of atmospheric chemistry models to control strategies.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 132A and CHEM 132B and CHEM 132C

title: Multi-Phase Atmospheric Chemistry
description: Chemical and physical processes leading to the production, aging, and removal of atmospheric particles. Multi-phase processes involving gases, particles, water droplets, and environmental surfaces. Approaches for modeling these processes with applications to control strategies.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 245A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Special Topics in Atmospheric Chemistry

prerequisiteText: CHEM 245B with a minimum grade of B-
repeatability: May be taken unlimited times as topics vary

title: Separations and Chromatography
description: Introduction to modern separation techniques such as gas chromatography, high-performance liquid chromatography, supercritical fluid chromatography, capillary electrophoresis, and field flow fractionation. Applications of these separation strategies are discussed.

title: Current Problems in Analytical Chemistry
description: Surveys current research challenges in analytical chemistry. Topics include electrochemistry, chromatography, spectroscopy, and mass spectrometry.

title: Electrochemistry
description: Fundamentals of electrochemistry including thermodynamics and the electrochemical potential, charge transfer kinetics, and mass transfer. Methods based on controlled potential and controlled current are described; the effects of slow heterogeneous kinetics and the perturbation caused by homogeneous chemistry are discussed.

title: Analytical Spectroscopy
description: Advanced treatment of spectroscopic techniques and instrumentation. Atomic and molecular absorption, emission, and scattering processes and their application to quantitative chemical analysis are outlined. Puts different spectroscopic techniques in perspective and demonstrates most appropriate applications to analytical problems.

title: Optics I - Physical Optics and Electromagnetic Theory
description: Treatment of optical phenomena and interactions between electromagnetic radiation and matter using fundamental electromagnetic laws, with applications to modern spectroscopic methods.

title: Optics II – Light-Matter Interaction and Advanced Spectroscopy
description: Advanced treatment of interactions between electromagnetic radiation and matter, with applications to linear spectroscopy, time-resolved nonlinear methods, high-power light-matter interactions, and optical parametric processes.
prerequisiteText: CHEM 249A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Computational Chemistry
description: Basic concepts, methods, and techniques in computational chemistry: density functional and wavefunction theory, molecular property calculations, analysis tools, potential energy surfaces, vibrational effects, molecular dynamics simulations.

title: Computational Chemistry Laboratory

prerequisiteText: CHEM 250 with a minimum grade of B-

title: The Formation of Ancient Greek Society: Early Greece
description: A survey of ancient Greek civilization from its origins in the Bronze Age to the mid-Archaic period. Examines political and social history, as well as literature, art, religion, and archaeological remains.

title: The Formation of Ancient Greek Society: Late Archaic and Classical Greece
description: A survey of ancient Greek civilization from the Late Archaic period to the Classical period. Focuses on major institutions and cultural phenomena as seen through the study of ancient Greek literature, history, archaeology, and religion.

title: The Formation of Ancient Greek Society: Fourth-Century and Hellenistic Greece
description: A survey of ancient Greek civilization from the fourth century BCE through to the Hellenistic period. Focuses on major institutions and cultural phenomena as seen through the study of ancient Greek literature, history, archaeology, and religion.

title: The Formation of Ancient Roman Society: Origins to Roman Republic
description: A survey of the development of Roman civilization from its eighth century BCE beginnings to the civil wars of the first century BCE. Examines political and social history, as well as literature, art, architecture, and religion.

title: The Formation of Ancient Roman Society: Roman Empire
description: A survey of Roman civilization from Augustus’s consolidation of power following the civil wars of the first century BCE to the crisis of the third century CE. Includes social history, literature, art, architecture, and religion.

title: The Formation of Ancient Roman Society: The Fall of Rome
description: A survey of Roman civilization from the crisis of the third century CE to the so-called “fall of Rome” in 476 CE. Examines political and social history, as well as literature, art, architecture, and religion.

description: Examines the importance of subaltern studies for the study of modern history, postcolonial studies, social theory, and cultural studies. Also considers subaltern studies within a larger set of debates in structuralism, post-structuralism, Marxism, and post-Marxism.
restriction: Graduate students only.

title: Crossing Borders: Empire and Im/migration
description: Utilizes historically-based intersectional analysis to explore the connections between U.S. empire and migration; border formation and incarceration; as well as identity and structural forms of hierarchy.
restriction: Graduate students only.

title: Freedom Dreams: Subaltern Forms of Resistance
description: Explores how subjugated peoples have creatively and collectively resisted oppression. Explores how individuals and communities envision a more just society, experiment with political strategies, and create meaningful legacies.
restriction: Graduate students only.

title: Resistance Spaces
description: Examines the relationship between the production of space and the operation of power in cultural studies and critical social theory.
restriction: Graduate students only.

title: Ethics, Erotics, and Will: Gendered Black Politics, Sexualized Racisms, and the Humanities
description: Introduces doctoral students to an interdisciplinary conversation about black queer sexuality and black heteropatriarchy. Uses disciplinary formations as a tool for understanding knowledge formations about the shifting relations that constitute sexuality, gender, and racial blackness.
restriction: Graduate students only.

title: Afro-Pessimism and the Status of the Subject
description: Afro-Pessimism theorizes the Black as a being against which all other beings become legible as human subjects. Focuses on either the subject of psychoanalysis or the subject of capital accumulation in their explorations of the antagonism between Blackness.

title: Introduction to Performance Studies

restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Abnormal Psychology
description: Introduction to psychopathology and behavioral deviations, and the concepts of theories regarding these conditions.
prerequisiteText: COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4 or COGS 9C or PSCI 11C
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Developmental Psychology
description: A general introduction to the study of the physical, intellectual, social, and emotional development of the child from birth to adulthood.
prerequisiteText: COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4 or COGS 9A or PSCI 11A
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: History of Psychology
description: A history of the development of various schools and systems of psychological thought.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or (COGS 9A or PSCI 11A) and (COGS 9B or PSCI 11B) and (COGS 9C or PSCI 11C)
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Personality Theories
description: A survey of the evolution of personality theory during this century. An overview of major perspectives in the field, with special attention to Freud, Jung, and Adler.
prerequisiteText: COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4 or COGS 9C or PSCI 11C
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Psychology of Sleep and Consciousness
description: Covers the physiology, neurochemistry, and neuroanatomy associated with sleep, contemporary sleep theory, REM and NREM, phenomenology, sleep disorders, examination of differences between conscious and unconscious cognitive function, the history of sleep and dream theories from ancient time to present day.
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Clinical Psychology
description: Provides overview of the clinical psychology field including theories and techniques used in counseling and testing.
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Organizational/Industrial Psychology
description: Introduction to applied psychology in organizations, including personnel testing, selection, training and evaluation, job and classification analysis, job satisfaction and motivation, organizational development, leadership, market research, and consumer psychology. Potential ethical problems are discussed.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or (COGS 9A or PSCI 11A) or (COGS 9B or PSCI 11B) or (COGS 9C or PSCI 11C)
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Creativity
description: Introduction to creativity, addressing creativity with respect to cognition, development, neuroscience, education, personality, motivation, and social aspects of creativity.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or ((COGS 9A or PSCI 11A) and (COGS 9B or PSCI 11B) and (COGS 9C or PSCI 11C))
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Sports Psychology
description: Discusses the field of sports psychology with an emphasis on clinical practice including motivation, goal setting, performance skills, and mental skills. Discusses and utilizes a wide range of techniques designed to enhance performance and manage problems among athletes.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or (COGS 9C or PSCI 11C)
restriction: Psychology majors and Cognitive Sciences majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Psychology of Violence
description: Discusses the psychology of violence and aggression with an emphasis on understanding the psychological, social, and physiological roots of violent and aggressive behavior. Psychological treatment techniques and strategies for prevention of aggressive and violent behavior are also discussed.
prerequisiteText: COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4 or COGS 9C or PSCI 11C
restriction: Psychology majors and Cognitive Sciences majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Moral Psychology
description: Survey course studying moral psychology and philosophy. Empirical research from psychology is supplemented with texts from philosophy for better grounding in philosophical theory.
prerequisiteText: COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4 or COGS 9B or PSCI 11B
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Personality Disorders
description: The history of personality disorder classification; defining characteristics of each disorder; the causes, courses, and outcomes of personality disorders; and information regarding assessment, prevention, and treatments of these disorders.
prerequisiteText: PSCI 11C or COGS 9C

title: Perception and Sensory Processes
description: A general introduction to the scientific study of sensory processes and perceptual phonomena, with special emphasis in the visual systems.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or (COGS 9A or PSCI 11A)
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Neuroscience of Perception
description: Introduces the principles that human perception is determined by the properties of brain circuitry and that these brain circuits evolved to interpret the properties of the physical environment to explore human perception from peripheral sensory organs to cortical processing.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or (COGS 9A or PSCI 11A)
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Vision
description: Visual perception and the anatomy and physiology of the visual system. Topics include the retina and the visual pathway; visual sensitivity; color vision; spatial vision; motion perception; and the development of the visual system.
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors, Psychology majors, and School of Biological Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Hearing
description: Auditory perception, the anatomy and physiology of the auditory system, and the physics of sound. Topics include neural transduction of sound, sensitivity, sound localization, complex sound perception, and hearing loss.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 9A or PSCI 11A) and (COGS 9B or PSCI 11B)
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Special Topics in Perception and Sensory Processes
description: Studies in selected areas of perception and sensory processes. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
prerequisiteText: Prerequisites vary.
repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.
restriction: Cognitive Sciences Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Psychology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.

title: Judgment and Decision Making
description: The psychology of human decision making. Theories, models, experiments, and data that inform how people make choices, judgments, and other decisions. Topics include optimality and bias, mental simulation, learning and feedback, expertise, emotional effects, and group decision making.
prerequisiteText: COGS 9A and COGS 9B
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Learning and Decision Making
description: The psychological and neural bases of learning about and interacting with the world. Topics include shaping of behavior by rewards and punishments, abstraction of relational information, goal-directed versus habitual decision strategies, social knowledge transmission, and behavioral and substance addictions.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or (COGS 9A or PSCI 11A)
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Human Memory
description: Developments in the area of memory; history of memory research; theories of the nature of memory. Visual memory, recognition memory, high-speed scanning, free recall, short-term memory, mnemonics, retrieval, relationship of memory to thinking. Selected theoretical formulations for memory.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or (COGS 9B or PSCI 11B)
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Human Problem Solving
description: Modern developments in the psychology of human problem solving. Topics include concept identification, arithmetic, sets, logic puzzles, story problems, group problem solving, and theorem proving.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or (COGS 9B or PSCI 11B)
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: MATLAB Programming
description: MATLAB is a mathematical software package for solving quantitative problems often encountered in experimental psychology. Topics include rudiments of programming, statistical analysis of data, matrix algebra, signal processing, graphic visualization, and simulated models of cognitive and perceptual processes.

title: Scientific Python for Research
description: Introduces Python for data analysis and modeling encountered in cognitive science and neuroscience. Topics include data structures, execution control, graphic visualization, and interaction with sound and display interfaces. Application in statistical analysis, model simulation, and stimulus presentation and experimental control.
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Psychology of Language
description: Examines language using the tools of experimental psychology. From sounds to words to spoken and written sentences, explores how language is used in real time, and how its use reveals how it is represented in the mind.
prerequisiteText: LSCI 3 and (LSCI 51 or COGS 56L)

title: African American Psychology
description: Historical overview of the development of black psychology and the African American frame of reference. Topics include personality development, psychological assessment, issues in education, black mental health, and the role of the African American psychologist in the community.

title: Computational Methods for Language Research
description: Focuses on computational methods useful for language research. Students become familiar with software and programming languages used for extracting information from electronic datasets and for creating basic simulations of linguistic cognition. No prior programming experience assumed.
prerequisiteText: COGS 150 or LSCI 155 or COGS 156A or LSCI 151

title: Introduction to Cognitive Neuroscience
description: Introduction to the neural basis of human perceptual, motor, and cognitive abilities. Topics include sensory perception, motor control, memory, language, attention, emotion, frontal lobe function, functional brain imaging, and neuropsychological disorders.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or ((COGS 9A or PSCI 11A) and (COGS 9B or PSCI 11B))
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Brain Disorders and Behavior
description: Examines the localization of human brain functions and the effects of neurological disorders on psychological functions such as perception, motor control, language, memory, and decision-making.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or (COGS 9A or PSCI 11A) and (COGS 9B or PSCI 11B) or BIO SCI 35 or BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A
restriction: Biological Sciences majors, Cognitive Sciences majors, and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Language and the Brain
description: Research analysis on biological bases of human linguistic capacity. Development, focusing on hemispheric specialization, plasticity; localization of specific linguistic functions in adults, with emphasis on study of aphasias; relation of linguistic capacity to general cognitive capacity, considering research on retardation.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or (COGS 9A or PSCI 11A) and (COGS 9B or PSCI 11B) or BIO SCI 35 or BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A

title: Hearing and the Brain
description: An overview of brain mechanisms of hearing, including perception of simple sounds, speech, and music. Begins with sound itself, and looks at processing by the ear, auditory pathways, auditory cortex, and beyond. Also auditory development, learning, and clinical issues.

title: Evolution of Language and Music
description: Focuses on the biological evolution of two rather unique human traits: language and music. No other species is capable of “doing” language or music with the complexity that humans can.

title: Human Neuropsychology
description: A survey of human brain disorders using a clinical case study approach to illustrate fundamental issues in studying brain and behavior. Topics include sensory deficits, attentional neglect, amnesia, cortical organization, clinical psychopathology, and more.
prerequisiteText: BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A or COGS 9A or PSCI 11A

title: Metacognition
description: Critical analysis of primary literature targeting metacognition in perception and memory, including neural correlates. Coverage includes behavioral experimental design, computational models, psychophysics, noninvasive neuroimaging, and neural stimulation approaches.
prerequisiteText: (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or ((COGS 9A or PSCI 11A) and (COGS 9B or PSCI 11B))
restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Psychological Anthropology
description: Cultural differences and similarities in personality and behavior. Child-rearing practices and consequent adult personality characteristics, biocultural aspects of child development and attachment, culture and behavior evolutionary models, politically linked personality, cognitive anthropology, psychology of narrative forms, comparative national character studies.
prerequisiteText: ANTHRO 2A or (COGS 7A or PSCI 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or (COGS 9A and COGS 9B and COGS 9C) or (PSCI 11A and PSCI 11B and PSCI 11C)
restriction: Anthropology majors, Cognitive Sciences majors, Psychology majors, Anthropology minors, and Medical Anthropology minors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Chicano/Latino Families
description: Introduction to the research, literature, and issues surrounding the topic of Chicano/Latino families including cultural history, contemporary issues, organization of family, traditions, lifestyles, values, beliefs, generational differences, gender issues, ethnic identity, evolution of demographic patterns, current economic and political standings.

title: Political Psychology
description: Examination of how psychological theory and research may be used to better understand political thought and behavior. Drawing on theories of learning, cognition, and personality, discusses such topics as the formation of political attitudes, and the process of political decision-making.

title: Deviance
description: Perspectives on deviance and criminality in behavior, institution, community, and myth. The suitability of contemporary theories of deviant behavior.
restriction: Criminology, Law and Society majors, Social Ecology majors, Sociology majors, and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Forensic Psychology: Advanced Seminar
description: Focuses on the psychology of criminal offending, particularly violent behavior. Examines violence, sexual offending, and mental disorder related to crime with regard to clinical assessment and treatment; mental health services within forensic institutions.
prerequisiteText: (PSCI 9 or PSCI 11C or COGS 7A or COGS 9C) and PSCI 102C and (PSCI 178S or CRM/LAW C149)

title: Social Psychology of Networks
description: Review of network methods used in small group and organizational research. Discussion of social psychological literature relevant to the network of study of cognitive social structure, exchange/communication, identity negotiation, and social control. Case study of network datasets exemplifies research issues.

title: Statistical Models for Cognitive Sciences II
description: An introduction to statistical estimation and statistical inference. Topics include sufficiency and the Rao-Blackwell Theorem, completeness and the Lehmann-Scheffe Theorem. The method of maximum likelihood is explored in some detail. Inference in linear models covers regression and analysis of variance.

title: Statistical Models for Cognitive Sciences III
description: Discussion of the fundamentals of statistical inference and computational implementations of common statistical models.

title: Applied Mathematics for Cognitive Sciences
description: Covers the basics of linear systems analysis, focusing on linear algebra, Fourier analysis, differential equations, and elementary signal processing. Applications in Cognitive Science and Cognitive Neuroscience research are developed.
restriction: Graduate students only.

description: Introduction to statistical learning for scientific research. Topics include linear regression, logistic regression, model selection, cross-validation, ridge and Lasso regularization, classification trees, ensemble methods, random forests, unsupervised learning, PCA, k-means clustering, Gaussian mixture models, and PLS regression.
prerequisiteText: Required: Knowledge of calculus, computer programming, and undergraduate-level statistics
restriction: Cognitive Neuroscience majors and Cognitive Sciences majors only

title: Neural Networks and Machine Learning
description: An introduction and review of the current state of the art in neural networks and machine learning with specific emphasis of applications to behavioral and neuroscience data analysis and modeling.

title: Cognitive and Brain Sciences I: Topics in Perception
description: Discusses models of cognition and evidence linking cognition and the brain. Focus is on visual, auditory, and somatic perception and bottom-up mechanisms of attention.
repeatability: May be taken unlimited times as topics vary

title: Cognitive and Brain Sciences II: Topics in Cognition
description: Discusses models of cognition and evidence linking cognition and the brain. Focus is on emotion, top-down attention, goal-directed behavior, categorization, judgment, and decision-making.
repeatability: May be taken unlimited times as topics vary

title: Cognitive and Brain Sciences III: Topics in Learning and Development
description: Discusses experimental data, formal models of learning, and evidence linking learning and development to its neural substrates. Topics include Pavlovian and instrumental conditioning, language acquisition, causal reasoning, perceptual learning, category formation, and structure learning.

Covers physical aspects of sound; subcortical auditory processing; aspects of sensation and perception such as sensitivity, sound localization, and complex-sound recognition; neuroscientific studies of cortical function; and abnormal auditory processing.

description: Focuses on psychosocial dynamics of today's adolescents in America emphasizing the quest for identity, independence, values, and sexual orientation. The influence of society, family, school, and peers is analyzed. Strategies for helping troubled adolescents are discussed.

title: Introduction to Functional MRI
description: Describes the fundamentals of imaging the human brain function using functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI). Topics include basic fMRI physics, experimental design, and data acquisition and analysis.

description: Introduction to computational neuroscience. Mathematical models of single neurons, neural circuits, thalamocortical systems, and cortical mass action can stimulate single-unit, local field potential, and EEG dynamics. These models are used to investigate mechanisms of sensation, motor control, attention, and consciousness.

title: Cognitive Robotics
description: Introduces concepts for studying cognitive function by embedding brain models on robotic platforms. Topics include robot construction, computer programming, and the notion of embodiment. Students construct simple robots and program these robots to perform different behaviors.

Examples of embedded computing in real-world application domains. Simple programming using an embedded systems development environment.

school: Donald Bren School of Information and Computer Sciences
title: Programming in Multitasking Operating Systems
description: User- and systems-level programming of modern Internet-connected, multi-user, multitasking operating systems. Shells, scripting, filters, pipelines, programmability, extensibility, concurrency, inter-process communication. Concrete examples of a modern operating system (such as, but not necessarily, Unix programmed in C) are used.
prerequisiteText: I&C SCI 46 with a minimum grade of C and I&C SCI 51 with a minimum grade of C. Recommended: COMPSCI 143A
restriction: Computer Science and Engineering majors and School of Information and Computer Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment

school: Donald Bren School of Information and Computer Sciences
title: Internet of Things (IoT) Software and Systems
description: Introduction to the Internet of Things (IoT) from a systems and software perspective. IoT ecosystem including sensors, embedded CPUs, networking protocols, software, cloud services, and security and privacy requirements. IoT use cases, system design, and programming project.
prerequisiteText: I&C SCI 33
restriction: Computer Science and Engineering majors and School of Information and Computer Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment

school: Donald Bren School of Information and Computer Sciences
title: Digital Logic Design
description: Boolean algebra. Design/analysis of combinational and sequential systems using SSI/MSI/LSI modules. Number systems. Error detecting and correction codes. Arithmetic algorithms. Hardware/firmware implementation of algorithms.
prerequisiteText: I&C SCI 33 with a minimum grade of C and I&C SCI 51 with a minimum grade of C and I&C SCI 6B and I&C SCI 6D
restriction: Computer Science and Engineering majors and School of Information and Computer Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment

school: Donald Bren School of Information and Computer Sciences
title: Computer Architecture
description: Design of computer elements; ALU, control unit, and arithmetic circuits. Memory hierarchy and organization. Caches. Function unit sharing and pipelining. I/O and interrupt processing. RTL and behavioral modeling using hardware description languages. Microprocessor organization and implementation techniques.
prerequisiteText: I&C SCI 51

description: Introduction to standard integrated circuits. Construction and debugging techniques. Design of digital systems using LSI and MSI components. Practical use of circuits in a laboratory environment, including implementation of small digital systems such as arithmetic modules, displays, and timers.
prerequisiteText: COMPSCI 151
restriction: School of Info & Computer Sci students have first consideration for enrollment. Computer Science Engineering Majors have first consideration for enrollment.

school: Donald Bren School of Information and Computer Sciences
title: Computer Design Laboratory
description: Underlying primitives of computer instruction sets. Principles of microprogramming. Microprogramming. Microprograms written for one or more systems. Typical microprogramming applications discussed and implemented or simulated.
prerequisiteText: COMPSCI 151 or COMPSCI 152
restriction: Computer Science and Engineering majors and School of Information and Computer Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
